title: Vector
notes:
Introduction to Vectors

A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction and obeys the triangle law of vector addition. Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, and electric field. A scalar quantity has only magnitude and no direction; examples include mass, time, temperature, speed, work, energy, and distance. Vectors are represented by boldface letters (e.g., v) or with an arrow overhead (\vec{v}). The magnitude of a vector \vec{v} is written as |\vec{v}| or simply v.

Types of Vectors

Equal vectors: Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and same direction (e.g., \vec{a} and \vec{b} are equal if |\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| and they are parallel). Negative vector: A vector with the same magnitude but opposite direction to a given vector (\vec{-a}). Null (zero) vector: A vector with zero magnitude; its direction is undefined (\vec{0}). Unit vector: A vector of magnitude 1 along a given direction, written as \hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}. In Cartesian coordinates, the standard unit vectors are \hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k} along the x, y, z axes. Parallel and antiparallel vectors: Vectors along the same line (parallel if same sense, antiparallel if opposite). Position vector: Vector joining the origin O to a point P, written as \vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}. Collinear vectors: Vectors lying along the same straight line. Coplanar vectors: Vectors lying in the same plane.

Vector Addition — Triangle and Parallelogram Laws

The triangle law: If two vectors \vec{a} and \vec{b} are represented by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant \vec{R} = \vec{a} + \vec{b} is represented by the third side taken in the opposite order. The parallelogram law: If two vectors act from the same point and are represented by adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram passing through that point. For two vectors \vec{a} and \vec{b} at angle \theta, the magnitude of the resultant is:

$$R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos\theta}$$

and the direction \alpha (angle with \vec{a}) is given by:

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{b\sin\theta}{a + b\cos\theta}$$

Special cases: Parallel (\theta = 0°) → R = a + b; Antiparallel (\theta = 180°) → R = |a - b|; Perpendicular (\theta = 90°) → R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}. Vector addition is commutative (\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{b} + \vec{a}) and associative ((\vec{a} + \vec{b}) + \vec{c} = \vec{a} + (\vec{b} + \vec{c})).

Subtraction and Resolution of Vectors

Vector subtraction: \vec{a} - \vec{b} = \vec{a} + (-\vec{b}); reverse the direction of \vec{b} and add. Resolution of a vector: Any vector \vec{A} in a plane can be resolved into two perpendicular components along x and y axes: A_x = A\cos\theta, A_y = A\sin\theta, where \theta is the angle with the x-axis. Then A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2} and \tan\theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}. In unit vector notation: \vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}. In 3D: \vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k} with A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}. The direction cosines are \cos\alpha = A_x/A, \cos\beta = A_y/A, \cos\gamma = A_z/A, satisfying \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1.

Scalar (Dot) Product

The scalar product of two vectors \vec{a} and \vec{b} is defined as \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = ab\cos\theta, where a = |\vec{a}|, b = |\vec{b}|, and \theta is the angle between them (0 \le \theta \le \pi). The result is a scalar. Properties: (1) Commutative: \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}. (2) Distributive: \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}. (3) \vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = a^2. (4) For perpendicular vectors, \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0. (5) In component form: \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z. Applications: Work done W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s}, power P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}, projection of \vec{a} on \vec{b} = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}.

Vector (Cross) Product

The vector product of \vec{a} and \vec{b} is a vector \vec{c} = \vec{a} \times \vec{b} with magnitude |\vec{c}| = ab\sin\theta and direction perpendicular to the plane of \vec{a} and \vec{b}, given by the right-hand rule (curl fingers from \vec{a} to \vec{b}, thumb gives direction). Properties: (1) Anti-commutative: \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = -\vec{b} \times \vec{a}. (2) Distributive: \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \times \vec{b} + \vec{a} \times \vec{c}. (3) For parallel vectors, \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}. (4) In component form using determinant: \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \end{vmatrix}. Applications: Torque \vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}, angular momentum \vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}, magnetic force \vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}, area of parallelogram = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|.

Scalar Triple Product

The scalar triple product of three vectors \vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c} is \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = [\vec{a} \; \vec{b} \; \vec{c}]. It represents the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors: V = |\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})|. Properties: (1) Cyclic permutation: [\vec{a} \; \vec{b} \; \vec{c}] = [\vec{b} \; \vec{c} \; \vec{a}] = [\vec{c} \; \vec{a} \; \vec{b}]. (2) Interchanging any two vectors changes sign. (3) If vectors are coplanar, the scalar triple product is zero. (4) In component form: [\vec{a} \; \vec{b} \; \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \\ c_x & c_y & c_z \end{vmatrix}.

Vector Triple Product

The vector triple product is \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}). It satisfies the BAC-CAB rule: \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{b}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}) - \vec{c}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}). Note that \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) \neq (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c} in general. The result lies in the plane of \vec{b} and \vec{c}. This is useful in deriving formulas for torque, angular acceleration, and in rigid body dynamics.

Applications in Physics

Vectors are essential across mechanics and electromagnetism. Displacement \vec{s} = \vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i. Velocity \vec{v} = d\vec{r}/dt. Acceleration \vec{a} = d\vec{v}/dt. Force \vec{F} = m\vec{a} (Newton's 2nd law). Momentum \vec{p} = m\vec{v}. Angular velocity \vec{\omega}, torque \vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}, angular momentum \vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}. In electromagnetism: Electric field \vec{E}, magnetic field \vec{B}, Lorentz force \vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B}), Poynting vector \vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}. Understanding vectors is foundational for all of physics.
confusion: Vectors are not just arrows; they are mathematical objects obeying specific addition laws — A quantity with magnitude and direction is a vector only if it follows the triangle/parallelogram law of addition (e.g., current has magnitude and direction but is a scalar).
The magnitude of the sum is NOT the sum of magnitudes — |\vec{a} + \vec{b}| \neq |\vec{a}| + |\vec{b}| in general; it equals a + b only when vectors are parallel (\theta = 0°).

Dot product gives a SCALAR, cross product gives a VECTOR — Students often confuse the results; dot product measures 'how much one vector goes along another' (projection), cross product measures 'how much they are perpendicular' (area of parallelogram).
The cross product is NOT commutative — \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = -\vec{b} \times \vec{a}; the order matters and determines the direction via the right-hand rule.
The angle in dot/cross product is ALWAYS the smaller angle (0° to 180°) — Never use angles > 180°; cos(200°) = cos(160°), but sin(200°) = -sin(20°), which would flip the direction incorrectly.
A vector can have zero component in one direction but non-zero magnitude — A vector \vec{v} = 3\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} has magnitude 3, not zero; zero component means no projection along that axis.
Unit vectors \hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k} are dimensionless — They represent pure direction; their magnitude is 1 (no units), so multiplying by a scalar gives the vector its units.
Resolution of a vector is NOT unique unless axes are specified — The same vector has different components in different coordinate systems; always state the reference axes.
practice: Two forces \vec{F}_1 = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} N and \vec{F}_2 = -2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} N act on a particle. Find the resultant force and its magnitude. [Solution: \vec{R} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 = (1)\hat{i} + (9)\hat{j} N; |\vec{R}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{82} \approx 9.06 N.]

A displacement vector \vec{s} = 6\hat{i} - 8\hat{j} m. Find its magnitude and the angle it makes with the positive x-axis. [Solution: |\vec{s}| = \sqrt{6^2 + (-8)^2} = 10 m; \tan\theta = -8/6 = -4/3 \Rightarrow \theta = -53.1° or 306.9° (4th quadrant).]

Find the angle between vectors \vec{a} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} and \vec{b} = 5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}. [Solution: \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 15 - 48 = -33; |\vec{a}| = 5, |\vec{b}| = 13; \cos\theta = -33/65 \Rightarrow \theta = \cos^{-1}(-33/65) \approx 120.5°.]

A force \vec{F} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} N acts on a particle moving from (2, 1) m to (5, 6) m. Find the work done. [Solution: \vec{s} = (5-2)\hat{i} + (6-1)\hat{j} = 3\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} m; W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s} = 4(3) + 3(5) = 12 + 15 = 27 J.]

Find the area of the parallelogram formed by \vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k} and \vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}. [Solution: Area = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|. \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(1+6) - \hat{j}(2-3) + \hat{k}(-4-1) = 7\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 5\hat{k}; Area = \sqrt{49+1+25} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3} \text{ sq. units}.]

Show that vectors \vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}, \vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}, \vec{c} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k} are coplanar. [Solution: Scalar triple product [\vec{a} \; \vec{b} \; \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 1(15-16) - 2(10-12) + 3(8-9) = -1 + 4 - 3 = 0. Since it's zero, they are coplanar.]

A particle moves with velocity \vec{v} = (3t^2)\hat{i} + (4t)\hat{j} m/s. Find acceleration at t = 2 s. [Solution: \vec{a} = d\vec{v}/dt = (6t)\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}; at t=2, \vec{a} = 12\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} m/s^2; |\vec{a}| = \sqrt{144+16} = \sqrt{160} = 4\sqrt{10} \approx 12.65 m/s^2.]

Find a unit vector perpendicular to both \vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} and \vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}. [Solution: \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(1-2) - \hat{j}(2+1) + \hat{k}(-4-1) = -\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}. Magnitude = \sqrt{1+9+25} = \sqrt{35}. Unit vector = \frac{-\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}}{\sqrt{35}}.]

A boat crosses a river 100 m wide flowing at 2 m/s. The boat's speed in still water is 5 m/s. Find (a) the time to cross, (b) the downstream drift. [Solution: (a) Time = width / v_y = 100/5 = 20 s. (b) Drift = v_river * time = 2 * 20 = 40 m.]
universalFacts: The word 'vector' comes from Latin 'vehere' meaning 'to carry' — introduced by William Rowan Hamilton (1843) as part of quaternion algebra; Josiah Willard Gibbs and Oliver Heaviside later developed the modern vector analysis (1880s) separating scalar and vector parts, which became the standard in physics.

Vectors in physics are 'bound vectors' (fixed in space by their point of application) unlike 'free vectors' in pure mathematics — Force is a bound vector (point of application matters for torque); displacement is a free vector (only magnitude and direction matter).

NEB exam tip: Always draw a vector diagram for addition/subtraction problems — Even if you can solve algebraically, a diagram helps avoid sign errors and earns partial marks for 'conceptual understanding' in long-answer questions.

The right-hand rule for cross product has physical basis — It matches the direction of rotation in nature: torque \vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} gives the axis of rotation following the right-hand rule; angular velocity \vec{\omega} and angular momentum \vec{L} follow the same convention.

In relativity, 3-vectors become 4-vectors — Displacement becomes 4-position (ct, x, y, z), velocity becomes 4-velocity; dot product is replaced by Minkowski metric with signature (+,−,−,−) or (−,+,+,+). Class 11 vectors are the non-relativistic limit.

Vector calculus (div, grad, curl) extends vector algebra to fields — Maxwell's equations use \nabla \cdot \vec{E} = \rho/\epsilon_0, \nabla \times \vec{E} = -\partial\vec{B}/\partial t; these operators act on vector fields and are essential for Class 12 electromagnetism.

The scalar triple product gives the signed volume — [\vec{a} \; \vec{b} \; \vec{c}] = V (positive if right-handed system). This is the determinant of the matrix with vectors as rows; it's zero for coplanar vectors — a quick test for coplanarity in 3D geometry problems.

Connection to kinematics: Position, velocity, and acceleration are all vectors — In 2D projectile motion, resolve into x (constant v) and y (constant a = -g) components; vector addition of components reconstructs the parabolic trajectory.
